opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few different versions of that hypothesis, and it's worth separating them, because they make pretty different claims.

The strongest version would say that a Transformer trained on raw text ends up building something like the trees linguists draw: it identifies constituents, figures out which words combine with which, and maybe even uses different layers to build up larger and larger units, almost like a bottom-up parser spread across the depth of the network. That's an appealing picture, partly because it would mean the model rediscovered something linguists have argued for a long time, that sentences have hierarchical structure and not just linear order.

A weaker version, which I think is better supported, says that the model's internal representations *encode* information that is correlated with syntactic structure. If you train a probe, say a linear classifier or one of the structural probes that try to recover tree distances from the geometry of the embedding space, you can often pull out a lot of syntactic information: which words are heads, roughly how far apart two words are in the parse tree, and so on. And you see some layer-wise trends, where more local information like part of speech is more available earlier and more abstract relational information peaks somewhere in the middle layers.

But I'm cautious about moving from the second claim to the first. The fact that you can decode a tree from the representations doesn't mean the model is *using* that tree when it makes predictions. A sufficiently expressive probe can learn a lot on its own, and information can be present in a representation without being causally relevant to the model's behavior. So for me the more interesting test is behavioral and causal. Does the model behave as if it's sensitive to hierarchical structure, for example getting subject-verb agreement right across intervening clauses with distracting nouns, or generalizing in a hierarchical rather than a linear way when the training data is ambiguous between the two? And if you intervene on the representation that supposedly encodes the structure, does the behavior change in the way you'd predict?

The picture from that kind of work is mixed, and to me that's the honest answer. Models trained on enough data do a lot of things that look syntactically sophisticated, and they clearly aren't just tracking n-grams. But they also make errors that a system with a clean tree representation probably wouldn't make, and their generalization out of distribution is often less hierarchical than we'd like, especially when you control the amount of training data to something closer to what a child gets. So I'd say Transformers represent *something* that overlaps substantially with syntactic structure, but whether it's best described as trees, and whether it's organized across layers in the way the stronger hypothesis suggests, is still very much an open question.

r001.rationale: The response describes a possible layer-wise parsing picture but does not state that representing a tree requires at least as many layers as its depth.

r002.rationale: It describes layers building up “larger and larger units” in a bottom-up parser-like process.

r003.rationale: It notes weaker hierarchical generalization and model errors, but does not link those outcomes to insufficient depth forcing alternative strategies.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. The way I'd frame it is that there are really two different claims hiding inside that hypothesis, and it's worth pulling them apart.

The first claim is about what information is present. The work that kicked this off, Hewitt and Manning's structural probe, showed that if you take the vector representations from a model like BERT, you can learn a linear transformation under which the distance between two words' vectors approximates their distance in a dependency parse tree. And the layers where that works best are the middle layers, not the top or the bottom. So in that sense, yes, something that correlates with tree structure is linearly recoverable from the representations, and it's organized in a layer-wise way, with more lexical information lower down and something more abstract in the middle.

The second claim, which is the one people often slide into, is that the model is representing a tree in the way a linguist means it, and using that structure to compute the next word or whatever the task is. That's a much stronger claim, and I think the evidence for it is weaker than the enthusiasm sometimes suggests.

Part of the issue is methodological. A probe tells you that a certain kind of information is decodable from the representation. It doesn't tell you the model uses it. You can decode all sorts of things from these vectors, and some of them are just byproducts of the statistics of the training data. So there's been a lot of work on trying to tighten the inference, through control tasks, through causal interventions where you actually edit the representation and see whether behavior changes, and so on. That work is more mixed. You can sometimes find that the syntactic information the probe picks up isn't what's driving the model's predictions.

The other part is behavioral. My own interest has mostly been in asking whether these models actually behave as if they have hierarchical structure. The classic test cases are things like subject-verb agreement across an intervening noun phrase, or the kinds of structure-dependent generalizations that children make, like where you put the auxiliary when you form a question. And what you find is that large pretrained Transformers get a lot of these right, more than you might expect from a system with no inductive bias toward hierarchy, but they also fail in ways that a system with a genuine syntactic representation shouldn't. The failures track surface frequency and distance in ways that suggest the model is partly relying on linear heuristics, with something tree-like layered on top.

So my honest reading is that Transformers represent an approximation to syntactic structure, that it emerges from the data rather than from the architecture, and that it's distributed and somewhat redundant rather than being a clean tree sitting at one layer. The layer-wise story captures something real about the division of labor in the network, but I'd resist the picture of a parser living inside the model. It's more that the model has learned a bunch of features, some of which happen to be the features a parser would compute, because those features are useful for predicting words.

And I'd add that this is actually a scientifically interesting situation rather than a disappointing one. If you want to know what it takes to acquire syntax, a system that gets most of the way there from distributional statistics alone, without a built-in tree bias, is a pretty informative data point. The question that I find most pressing is what the remaining gap is made of, and whether it closes with scale or whether it reflects something that these models fundamentally aren't doing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses which layers encode tree-correlated information, but does not say that exact tree representation requires at least as many layers as the tree’s depth.

r002.rationale: It describes layer-wise differences in information, but does not explain that deeper layers progressively build larger syntactic constituents.

r003.rationale: It mentions linear heuristics and weaker syntactic behavior, but does not connect those strategies to Transformers being too shallow to represent the tree directly.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a couple of different claims that we should distinguish. One is that you can recover a syntactic tree from the representations of a Transformer. You take the representations at some layer, train a probe to predict syntactic relationships, and find that it does quite well. That tells us that information about syntax is available in those representations.

A stronger claim is that the model actually uses that information in doing whatever task it was trained to do, like predicting the next word. That doesn’t follow automatically from being able to decode a tree. The information could be there without playing a causal role in the prediction.

And then there’s a particularly literal interpretation of “across layers,” where each layer builds another level of the tree. I wouldn’t assume that’s how it works. Transformer layers and levels of a syntactic tree are different things, and syntactic information could be distributed across layers and across representations. So I’d treat this as a useful hypothesis, but we need to specify whether we mean that syntax is recoverable, that it’s used, or that the model implements a particular tree-building computation.

r001.rationale: The response does not state a minimum number of Transformer layers based on syntactic tree depth.

r002.rationale: It explicitly cautions against assuming each layer builds another tree level and does not say deeper layers build larger constituents.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss shallow Transformers using alternative strategies or how those strategies generalize.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a couple of different claims that we should distinguish. One is that you can recover information about syntactic structure from the representations at different layers of a Transformer. So you take those representations, train a probe to predict something about a syntactic tree, and see how well it does. If it does well, that tells you that the information is accessible to that probe.

The stronger claim is that the model actually uses that structure in processing a sentence. That doesn’t follow automatically. You might be able to recover a tree from the representations even if the model’s predictions depend on other properties of the sentence.

And I wouldn’t necessarily interpret the layers as literally building a tree from the bottom up, with each layer corresponding to another level of the tree. That’s a hypothesis you could test, but it’s more specific than saying that the representations encode syntax. The interesting question, to me, is whether those syntactic representations play a causal role: if we change them, does the model’s behavior change in the way we would expect?

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes recoverable syntactic information from stronger claims, but does not say that representing a tree requires at least as many layers as its depth.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says a bottom-up process with each layer corresponding to another tree level is a more specific hypothesis, without explaining progressively larger constituents.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss shallow Transformers using alternative strategies or compare how well those strategies generalize.
